See more: what do these inputs mean?

Allocation[i][j] is how many instances of resource Rj are held by Pi.

Request[i][j] is the outstanding request Pi needs to proceed, not its maximum possible future demand.

Available[j] is free resource instances; Total[j] is all instances of that resource.

For every resource, Total must equal Available plus all current allocations.

BEHIND THE ALGORITHM

From matrices to a verdict.

01

Initialize

Set Work to Available and initialize Finish based on whether each process holds resources.

02

Find & release

Find a process with Request ≤ Work, then add its Allocation back to Work.

03

Identify deadlock

Repeat until no more processes qualify. Unfinished processes are deadlocked.

See more: pseudocode and time complexity 
Work = Available
Finish[i] = (Allocation[i] is all zeros)
repeat:
    find i where not Finish[i] and Request[i] <= Work
    if none exists: break
    Work = Work + Allocation[i]
    Finish[i] = true
Deadlocked = all i with Finish[i] == false

A straightforward implementation scans up to P processes per successful completion, checking R resource types each time: O(P² × R) time and O(P + R) additional algorithmic space, excluding the input matrices and stored trace.

OS CONCEPTS

Learn more, only when you need it.

Core concepts for your project explanation, demonstration, and viva.

What is a deadlock?
A deadlock is a situation in which a set of processes cannot make progress because each is waiting for resources or events that other processes in the set must provide. For example, P0 holds R0 and requests R1 while P1 holds R1 and requests R0, with no free instances.
The four Coffman conditions
Mutual exclusion: at least one resource is non-shareable. Hold and wait: a process holds resources while requesting others. No preemption: resources cannot be forcibly reclaimed. Circular wait: a closed chain of processes waits for resources held by the next. All four are necessary for deadlock in the classic resource model.
Detection vs prevention vs avoidance
Prevention structurally eliminates at least one necessary condition. Avoidance uses advance knowledge of maximum claims and admits allocations only when the resulting state is safe. Detection allows allocation to proceed and periodically identifies existing deadlocks; recovery then takes action.
Is this Banker's Algorithm?
No. Banker's safety check uses Allocation, Max, and Need = Max − Allocation to decide whether a state is safe. This detector uses Allocation, current outstanding Request, and Available to identify processes currently deadlocked. An unsafe state does not necessarily mean a deadlock exists.
Single-instance and multiple-instance graphs
With one instance per resource type, a cycle in the resource allocation graph is necessary and sufficient for deadlock in the standard model. With multiple instances, a cycle alone is not sufficient; the matrix algorithm is more informative. The graph shown here represents resource types and labels counts rather than drawing each instance separately.
What happens after a deadlock is detected?
Possible recovery strategies include terminating all deadlocked processes, terminating them one at a time until the cycle breaks, or preempting resources where safe. Practical trade-offs include rollback, priority, work already completed, and starvation risk.
How do I explain the simulation in my viva?
Start by identifying P processes and R resource types. Explain the Allocation and Request matrices, Available vector, and Total validation. Run the detector, show how Work changes when an eligible process completes, then explain why unfinished processes remain blocked. Finally distinguish detection from Banker's avoidance.
